summary: Defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol is used to provision and manage domain names in a shared registry. It specifies the commands and their meanings for domains. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the EPP rulebook chapter about domain names, explaining how to register one, change it, renew it, or remove it from the registry.

questions: how do i create a domain with epp
what are epp domain status values
how does an epp domain transfer work
subtitle: How EPP commands apply to domain names: checking, registering, renewing, transferring and updating them in a registry.

tldr.problem: The base EPP protocol defines no objects, so registrars and registries needed an exact definition of how EPP commands work on Internet domain names.
tldr.mechanism: The mapping defines domain attributes (names, status values, validity periods, authorization information, name servers) and the XML for each EPP command applied to a domain, plus a way to report offline review outcomes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5731 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) that obsoletes RFC 4931. It needs RFC 5730 to be understood, and it relies on separate host and contact mappings.

today: RFC 5731 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 4931 and builds on RFC 5730.

sections.title: Domains, Hosts and Name Servers
sections.content:
This document is the domain name mapping for version 1.0 of EPP. RFC 5730 describes the command and response structures, and a thorough understanding of it is necessary to understand this mapping. The mapping obsoletes RFC 4931.

Domain objects have a superordinate relationship to subordinate host objects, whose mapping is in RFC 5732. For example, example.com is superordinate to ns1.example.com. Actions that do not preserve this relationship, such as some transfers, MUST be explicitly disallowed. A host can also be external, meaning its name is outside the namespace of the repository that uses it for delegation.

Name servers are given inside a <domain:ns> element, either as references to existing host objects (<domain:hostObj>) or as host attributes (<domain:hostAttr>) holding a name and optional IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. A server operator MUST use one form consistently: if it announces host object support in its greeting, it MUST NOT allow host attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain is like a house address, and name servers are the signposts that tell visitors where the house is. This part explains how to say which signposts belong to which address.

sections.title: Domain Object Attributes
sections.content:
A domain name must follow the host-name rules of RFC 952 and RFC 1123 and is written without the trailing dot. Contacts are identified by server-unique identifiers using the client identifier syntax from RFC 5730.

Every domain has at least one status value. Values prefixed client can be set and cleared by the sponsoring client, those prefixed server by the server, and the rest are server-managed. Examples are clientHold (DNS delegation information MUST NOT be published), clientDeleteProhibited, clientRenewProhibited, clientTransferProhibited, clientUpdateProhibited, inactive, ok and the pending family. ok MUST NOT be combined with any other status, and a pending status MUST NOT be combined with its matching prohibited status.

A domain MAY have a validity period, counted in years (y) or months (m), with a minimum value of 1 and a maximum of 99, though a server MAY support a lower maximum. Dates are UTC. Authorization information, described here as password-based, is assigned at creation and is used for transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each domain has little flags, like "locked" or "on hold", plus an expiry date. Some flags the owner's shop can flip, and some only the registry can flip.

sections.title: Query Commands
sections.content:
<domain:check> takes one or more fully qualified names and returns, for each, an avail attribute plus an optional reason. It is a hint only, since provisioning rules are ultimately server policy.

<domain:info> returns the name, the ROID, status values, registrant and contacts, name servers, subordinate hosts, the sponsoring client, and creation, expiry, update and transfer details. The sponsoring client, or a client giving valid authorization information, MUST receive all available information; for others, server policy decides which optional elements appear. A hosts attribute chooses all (the default), del, sub or none.

The <transfer> query (op="query") returns the state of the most recent transfer: who requested it and when, who should act on it, and the date by which an automatic response will happen if the request is still pending.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the registry "is this name free?", "tell me everything about this name", or "where is my move request up to?". The answers depend on who you are and what proof you show.

sections.title: Transform Commands
sections.content:
<domain:create> needs a name and authorization information, and can include an initial period, name servers, a registrant and other contacts. Host and contact objects MUST already be known to the server before they are associated with the domain. <domain:delete> SHOULD NOT succeed while subordinate hosts exist, and a server SHOULD signal that with error code 2305.

<domain:renew> carries the current expiry date (<domain:curExpDate>), which keeps repeated requests from renewing more than once, and an optional period. <domain:transfer> uses the op attribute from RFC 5730, and transferring a domain MUST implicitly transfer its subordinate hosts.

<domain:update> must carry at least one of <domain:add>, <domain:rem> or <domain:chg> unless an extension is present. Add and remove cover name servers, contacts and status values, while change covers the registrant and authorization information.

Unauthorized transform attempts MUST be rejected with response code 2201.
sections.plainLanguage: To get, renew, move or edit a name, you send a form with exactly the right boxes filled in. Moving a name also moves the signposts that live under it.

sections.title: Offline Review of Requested Actions
sections.content:
Transform commands are typically completed in real time, but a server MAY take one and delay the work for human or third-party review. It MUST then return result code 1001 and set a matching pending status, such as pendingCreate, on the domain.

When the review ends, the server queues a service message that clients fetch with <poll>. Its <resData> holds a <domain:panData> element with the name and a required paResult attribute (positive means approved and completed, negative means denied), the original transaction identifiers in <domain:paTRID>, and the review completion time in <domain:paDate>. The pending status MUST be removed and all involved clients notified.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a person at the registry has to look at your request first. You get a "we are checking" answer now, and a note later that says yes or no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authorization information is REQUIRED to create a domain and is used as an extra check in some query and transfer operations. Failing to protect it can lead to unauthorized transfers and unauthorized information release, so client and server MUST store and exchange it with high-grade encryption.

The mapping adds no other security services beyond those in RFC 5730 and the protocol layers EPP runs over.
sections.plainLanguage: The transfer password is like the key to your front door. If someone gets it, they can move your name away, so it has to be kept secret.

items.label: Normal
items.desc: No pending operations or prohibitions; set by the server and never combined with another status.

items.label: No delegation
items.desc: Delegation information has not been associated with the object.

items.label: Hold
items.desc: DNS delegation information MUST NOT be published.

items.label: No delete
items.desc: Requests to delete the object MUST be rejected.

items.label: No transfer
items.desc: Requests to transfer the object MUST be rejected.

items.label: Pending
items.desc: Command processed but the action is not yet completed; the same pattern applies to delete, renew, transfer and update.
